extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public interested in taste, poetry, and manners
extracted.subtask_short: periodical essay on taste and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: A set of short, didactic periodical essays giving prescriptive guidance and evaluative criteria for poetry (old ballads), social manners, and personal comportment (being a 'fine gentleman', avoiding distraction). Mixes literary criticism and moral instruction aimed at general cultured readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and poetical sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments in that Ballad are extremely natural and poetical, and full of majestick Simplicity which we admire in the greatest of the ancient Poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer thoughts and sentiments that arise naturally from the subject; such naturalness pleases both common people and refined tastes. Example: the ballad's stanzas exhibit natural, moving circumstances (e.g., widows washing wounds, kissing the dead). Anti-pattern: filling a song with epigrammatical turns and points of wit which may please a wrong taste but will not warm the common people's hearts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majestic simplicity reflecting classical models
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's tone and thought should resemble the majestic simplicity of ancient poets (Virgil, Homer), not by imitation of exact phrases but by being directed by the same poetical genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broad, elevated sentiments and structural likenesses (e.g., projecting consequences, long lists of the dead) that evoke the spirit of epic poets. Support claims by classical parallels where helpful. Example: comparisons to lines from the Aeneid and Horace are used to show affinity of thought and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epigrammatical turns; favor simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Had this old Song been filled with Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit, it might perhaps have pleased the wrong Taste of some Readers; but it would never have become the Delight of the common People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize clever, narrowly witty epigrams in works intended for broad emotional effect. Simplicity directed by nature has wider and more lasting appeal. Anti-pattern: 'Gothic' or affected ornament which pleases 'little wits' but spoils broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sounding language and sonorous numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Language is often very sounding, and the Numbers [sonorous; very sonorous].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to the musicality of verse—choice of smooth words, euphony, and rhythm that make lines 'sound' poetic. Examples in the ballad show how choice of words (e.g., landscape names, verbs of motion) creates a pleasing acoustic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of particularized detail within catalogues
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Catalogue of the Slain the Author has followed the Example of the greatest ancient Poets, not only in giving a long List of the Dead, but by diversifying it with little Characters of particular Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When listing many persons/events, diversify with small identifying particulars or mini-character sketches to keep the catalogue vivid and to humanize the list. Example: brief notes on Witherington or Sir Hugh Montgomery are used to individualize a catalogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance familiar names to preserve majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The familiar Sound in these Names destroys the Majesty of the Description; for this Reason I do not mention this Part of the Poem but to shew the natural Cast of Thought which appears in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse of colloquial or overly familiar names/details in high, majestic passages; such familiarity can undermine the elevated effect. Use familiarity sparingly and with intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projecting consequences across generations
rubrics_metrics.description: This way of considering the Misfortunes which this Battle would bring upon Posterity ... is wonderfully beautiful, and conformable to the Way of Thinking among the ancient Poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use poetic projection — considering effects on future generations — as a powerful device to enlarge the scope and poignancy of a subject. Example: stanza about unborn children rueing the hunting that led to battle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of thought in descriptive passages
rubrics_metrics.description: The third Stanza was never touched by any other Poet, and is such an one as would have shined in Homer or in Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek fresh angles on common subjects; an original and striking circumstance or turn of thought elevates a descriptive passage. Strive for unique details that nonetheless feel 'natural' to the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of diction and style to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The Language is often very sounding, and that the whole is written with a true poetical Spirit. If this Song had been written in the Gothic Manner ... it would not have hit the Taste of so many Ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style, diction and ornamentation to the subject and intended audience; avoid fashionable affectations (e.g., 'Gothic' manner) that conflict with the work's natural spirit. Use more 'gorgeous' apparel of language where it suits the subject, but avoid mismatches that alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the reader before particularization
rubrics_metrics.description: Witherington's Behaviour is in the same manner particularized very artfully, as the Reader is prepared for it by that Account which is given of him in the Beginning of the Battle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce or foreshadow salient features so that later particular details land effectively; setup makes later specific characterization feel earned and credible. Anti-pattern: dropping surprising particulars without context that feel unmotivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional, natural circumstances in narrative description
rubrics_metrics.description: What can be more natural or more moving than the Circumstances in which he describes the Behaviour of those Women who had lost their Husbands on this fatal Day?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include simple, believable human actions and emotions (washing wounds, kissing the dead) to create moving effects. Avoid theatrical exaggeration that undermines sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind's dress before body's dress (virtue over appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cloathing of our Minds certainly ought to be regarded before that of our Bodies. To betray in a Man's Talk a corrupted Imagination, is a much greater Offence against the Conversation of Gentlemen, than any Negligence of Dress imaginable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or forming oneself as a gentleman, prioritize internal virtues, manners and speech over outward dress. Coarse speech and corrupt imagination are graver faults than slovenly dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving reproach to humankind; show humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity obliges a Gentleman to give no Part of Humankind Reproach, for what they, whom they Reproach, may possibly have in Common with the most Virtuous and Worthy amongst us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A gentleman should avoid insulting whole classes or groups; exercise charity and restraint in speech and judgement. Anti-pattern: publicly belittling or mocking people for traits that could be shared with virtuous persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core virtues of a 'Fine Gentleman': generosity and bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a Fine Gentleman, is to be a Generous and a Brave Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate generosity, courage and magnanimity; these inner qualities produce a gracious ease and good-humour that appear in behaviour and speech. Example: firmness of mind, humanity, good-nature, and indifference to petty vanities produce the desirable ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graceful unconcern produced by fixed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm and unshaken Expectation of another Life, makes him become this; Humanity and Good-nature, fortified by the Sense of Virtue, has the same Effect upon him ... By a thorough Contempt of little Excellencies, he is perfectly Master of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and hold steady moral/philosophical principles (e.g., religious hope, sense of virtue) to produce genuine calmness and unaffected negligence; avoid affectation—true unconcern arises from solidity of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antipattern: the empty coxcomb / Vocifer
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocifer passes for a fine Gentleman. He is Loud, Haughty, Gentle, Soft, Lewd, and Obsequious by turns ... He is a professed Deluder of Women ... the empty Coxcomb has no Regard to any thing that is of it self Sacred and Inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the traits of the pretentious coxcomb: loudness, inconsistency, lewdness, obsequiousness, and insincerity. Such traits may deceive some but mark a lack of genuine breeding and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a law of life to avoid instability
rubrics_metrics.description: This proceeds from the Want of forming some Law of Life to our selves, or fixing some Notion of things in general, which may affect us in such Manner as to create proper Habits both in our Minds and Bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain consistent behaviour and temperament, deliberately fix guiding principles or a 'law of life' to cultivate steady habits. Without it, persons are subject to fluctuating humours and inconsistent conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observed human behavior deliberately (humour in governance)
rubrics_metrics.description: He would, by a skilful Cast of his Eye and half a Smile, make two Fellows who hated, embrace ... He gave Fortune to none but those whom he knew could receive it without Transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In positions of influence, observe and manage human tendencies wisely—use praise, favour or slight humorously and deliberately to correct vices and encourage virtues. Example: Pharamond uses observation and small public signals to reshape court behaviour; ethical caution advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish thoughtful absence from vacant distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: I distinguish a Man who is Absent, because he thinks of something else, from one who is Absent, because he thinks of nothing at all: The latter is too innocent a Creature to be taken notice of; but the Distractions of the former ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating someone's absent behaviour, determine whether it comes from deep reflection (which can be a sign of genius or engagement) or from vacuity (mere inattentiveness). Tailor social responses accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of distraction and their meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Either their Minds are wholly fixed on some particular Science ... or are wholly taken up with some Violent Passion ... or, lastly, these Distractions proceed from a certain Vivacity and Fickleness in a Man's Temper ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize common causes of 'being absent'—intense intellectual work, strong passions, or temperamentally rapid associative thought—and avoid simply condemning such persons without understanding context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countermeasures for inattentiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method I took to conquer it was a firm Resolution to learn something from whatever I was obliged to see or hear. ... I always make one of the Company I am in; though I say little myself, my Attention to others, and those Nods of Approbation which I never bestow unmerited, sufficiently shew that I am among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To cure absent-mindedness, resolve to extract learning from all encounters, consciously make oneself part of the company, practice attentive listening, and give small tokens of engagement (nods, brief remarks). This is practical advice to improve social presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antipattern examples of absent/distracted behaviour (Menalcas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Menalcas's absent acts: goes out half-shaved, wig caught in candlestick, takes another coach, swallows dice with wine, flings sand into the ink, mistakes letter superscriptions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these comic examples as cautionary anti-patterns; such slips expose one to ridicule and practical harm (robbery, mistaken identity). They illustrate how far distraction can undermine dignity and function.
